body:
| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.2.5** | Verify that passwords of any composition can be used, without rules limiting the type of characters permitted. There must be no requirement for a minimum number of upper or lower case characters, numbers, or special characters. | 1 | v5.0.be-2.1.9 |
| **6.2.8** | Verify that the application verifies the user's password exactly as received from the user, without any modifications such as truncation or case transformation. | 2 | v5.0.be-2.1.3 |
| **6.2.12** | Verify that passwords submitted during account registration or password changes are checked against a set of breached passwords. | 3 | v5.0.be-2.1.13 |


Some confusing levels

6.2.5 - problematic. For L1, it does not make sense (my application can and most likely be secure without meeting the requirement). Later, the rules for passwords do not make too much difference, as MFA is required.

Actually, I'm a bit surprised that it is SHALL NOT in [NIST 800-63B v4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html#passwordver):
> Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT impose other composition rules (e.g., requiring mixtures of different character types) for passwords.

I would say the direct impact on security is insufficient to be worth a requirement. It is kind of a message to end-users, that better use longer passwords (passphrases) instead of complicated to remember (but shorter and better target for brute-force) passwords.

More from NIST:
> The most notable form is composition rules, which require users to choose passwords that are constructed using a mix of character types (e.g., at least one digit, uppercase letter, and symbol). However, analyses of breached password databases reveal that the benefit of such rules is less significant than initially thought [[Policies]](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html#ref-policies), and the impacts on usability and memorability are severe.

So I conclude that "it is just not that helpful", but it does not make the application less secure. It is recommendation area.

---

6.2.8 - If to watch other stuff we have for L1 in this section, I think this should be L1.

---

6.2.12 - for L3, it should not have any meaningful impact, as L3 application must not rely on passwords anyway. From an impact perspective, it only makes sense for L1 as there is no MFA.

If to put the "just a task prioritisation" hat on, then it can be L2.

And maybe we should highlight extra in the chapter text (#2879), that it is just for task prioritisation, if the application uses only username and password for authentication, it is critical to implement all password-related requirements.

comments.body:
From #2879 was not addressed and it proving to be needed.
> Additionally, add a note to the section text that some password-related requirements are L1 because later MFA is used, and those are not that critical anymore. At the same time, it is important to understand that authentication asking only for username and password, however "strong" the rules for passwords or passphrases are, handling those securely depends on end-user behavior and the application security can not rely on that.

> So I conclude that "it is just not that helpful", but it does not make the application less secure. It is recommendation area.

I really don't want to get into this again. Composition rules lead to predictable password patterns which is why we disallow them. Additionally, restricting characters that can be used in a password is an anti-pattern and often indicates that they are being handled dangerously instead of being safely hashed.

If we really want to open this up again, we could try asking one of the original authors of the research: https://www.linkedin.com/in/reusablesec/

For the rest, let's discuss #2925 first
@elarlang to open a PR for L1, L1 and L2.

title: Levels for password-related requirements
